$comment: Data for /ops/library/state-of-play. A dated snapshot (2026-09-19), not live state — for whether a pipeline stage actually works, read /ops/standing. Regenerate rather than patch: append a new snapshot instead of editing numbers in place.
headline: The platform is ahead of the business.
lede: An engineering platform worth having now exists. Nothing has been sold through it. These are the numbers that decide what to do next.
northStar: Build the Hirobius web/automations agency: sign and ship paying client sites end-to-end — lead → generated site → publish → outreach → invoice. Infrastructure exists only in service of that.
scopeTest: The scope test on every ask: does this get a paying client site shipped sooner?
vitalsNote: Everything else on this page is commentary on those six figures. Lead counts are as recorded on 2026-09-17; the live verdict always comes from /ops/standing, which derives it from leads row counts rather than from any document — including this one.
builtAndWorking: A single fleet surface at /ops/standing, phone-operable and repo-filtered, deriving every verdict from live row counts. A Ralph autonomous loop with single-flight control, attempt caps and a supervised-path merge boundary. 63 registered guardrails with severity semantics, proof-of-firing fixtures and a registry that fails closed. A PII gate on pre-commit, commit messages, every PR and weekly. A design system published to npm with a Figma sync foundation. Visual regression now gated on pull requests and on main. That is a real platform. Measured against the scope test, it is also mostly indirect.

structural.triageTitle: 15 of 90 open issues are actionable by an agent
structural.triageBody: Every open issue across the six repos was triaged with adversarial verification — a second agent tried to refute each verdict, and 27 of 33 first-pass close/do-now calls were overturned. The split below is what survived that.

triageBuckets.meaning: An agent can finish it in one PR
A credential, a decision, a payment account, a real-world fact
Epic-shaped; must be split before anyone starts
Verdict was overturned without a clear replacement

structural.triageNote1: The count rose from 76 to 90 on purpose: two epics (ops#238, site-engine#153) were decomposed into 15 children. Decomposition inflates the number before it deflates it — it converts un-startable epics into shippable units.
structural.triageNote2: The related find, now measured: 86 remote branches have never had a pull request in any state, and 69 of them are agent branches that did work and stopped short of opening one. se#84's fix sat green and un-PR'd for two months before being recovered; se#107, ops#71 and ops#5 have the same shape. A branch with no PR is invisible to every surface we have, so some unknown share of the "blocked" 49 may already be finished. ops#407 asks for the report — not deletions, and not a 69-PR flood.
structural.sev1Title: ops#27 is the only sev1, and it is live
structural.sev1Body: ops, hds and site-engine are all public repositories, and client PII remains in git history. Prevention shipped; erasure did not. The gate also still matches generic patterns only, because the denylist does not exist yet — which is precisely how a client tenant's name reached a test fixture unflagged.

nextSteps: Spend one hour on the credentials table above. Highest ratio of outcome to effort anywhere on the board — every row releases work that is finished and idle.
Run the email crawler somewhere with egress. Until then, outreach v1 is not blocked on code. It is blocked on 262 missing addresses. Expect tuning, not a clean run.
Stripe. There is no path today from "shipped site" to "money received." It is the last unbuilt link in the north-star chain, and the one place where more infrastructure genuinely is the answer.
Then ops#27, using the rehearsed runbook in docs/ai/REPO-PROCEDURES.md.
handoffIntro: Every row is one pull request. Nothing here waits on a credential or a decision. Five of the original fifteen shipped on 19 September and are struck from the list: site-engine#205, #206 and #207, folio#9 and ops#399. Ten remain.

decisionsTitle: Three of the four big answers came in
decisionsIntro: These were the decisions with the largest downstream fan-out. Answered on 19 September:
decisions: site-engine#203 — build it now, all five. #205, #206 and #207 shipped the same day; #208–#210 are unblocked and queued.

ops#401 — ralph-auto is now conditional, not blanket. Tag it only on an issue whose definition of done names no supervised path. The blanket practice is what let PRs #368 and #362 merge lead-handling diffs unreviewed.

Engine v1 released — advanced from f645031 to a4f0c21, re-vendored in all three callers and verified live. Ralph#23 fixes orphan-branch recovery to pick the newest branch; Ralph#24 makes the kit-drift check compare against the engine revision actually running.
decisionsFourth: The fourth is still open and is 30 seconds of work: the hds release job is red on a repo setting — Settings → Actions → General → "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests". It is the only failing job on that repo's main.
safetyTitle: Two safety constraints that must not be reordered
safety: Ralph#25 before ops#402. The revenue-path boundary currently holds because risky issues simply aren't tagged ralph-auto — a human convention, not a mechanism. The ops#401 decision tightened that convention; it did not replace it. Flip auto-merge to default-on before the engine enforces paths and every green ralph/* PR self-merges, including one touching lib/leads/. Closing ops#238 in its stated order would delete the protection PR #375 added.

A new section variant is always an enum change, so it always needs the ops mirror (lib/schema + the vendored snapshot). A new optional field may not — se#84's analytics was safe only because its provider is a z.literal, and collectEnums() collects only kind === 'enum'.
